data.claim: run_piped leaks its stderr reader thread and the Popen's pipes when a descendant that left the process group keeps the stderr write end open after p.wait()
data.falsifier: close p.stderr from the caller side when the reader is still alive after the 1s join; the blocked read1 then stops and the fds are released
data.mechanism: drain() blocks in p.stderr.read1(); run_piped joins the reader only 1s and returns, so the daemon thread holds the Popen and its pipes alive until the descendant exits
data.probe_output: FAILED on unfixed code; 3 passed after the fix
data.question: Does run_piped leak its stderr reader thread and the Popen's pipes when a detached descendant holds the write end open?

evidence.note: CONFIRMED: run_piped leaks its stderr reader thread and Popen fds when a detached descendant holds the write end open; dbcdd 3 tests in tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py (test_a_blocked_stderr_reader_does_not_leak_the_pipe) FAIL on unfixed code and pass after closing p.stderr post-join. research note Rbcdeea0252.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix assumes that `p.stderr.close()` from the caller will unblock the daemon’s `p.stderr.read1()` call. On Linux/POSIX pipes, closing the read end from another thread does not wake a thread already blocked in `read(2)` on that pipe; the blocked read keeps waiting until every write end is closed. Concrete failing input: argv starts a child that exits after launching an escaped descendant which keeps the inherited stderr fd open; `work` returns `None`, `p.wait()` returns, `reader.join(1)` times out, and the new code calls `p.stderr.close()`. The reader remains blocked and still holds `p` and the pipe until that descendant exits, so the exact leak this change claims to fix persists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped (new `if reader.is_alive()` cleanup)

chunk_findings.detail: The new cleanup only runs on the `p.wait()` path. When `work` returns an answer after the child has exited, the early return path returns `PipedEnd(answer=answer)` without joining the reader or closing `p.stderr`; `finally` calls `stop_group(p)` only if `p.poll()` is None, and stopped group signaling does not kill an escaped descendant. Input: `work` returns an answer while a grandchild that called `os.setsid()` and kept the inherited stderr fd is still alive; `drain` remains blocked indefinitely and the same thread/Popen/pipe leak occurs despite this patch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped (`return PipedEnd(answer=answer)` path)

chunk_findings.detail: The only modification to `proc_server.py` in this part is an added blank line; the promised `run_piped` stderr-close/stop logic is absent. The new test `test_a_blocked_stderr_reader_does_not_leak_the_pipe` calls `PS.run_piped` with a `_Proc` whose `stderr` is a `_Pipe` and then asserts `proc.stderr.closed`. On the submitted code, `run_piped` joins the blocked stderr reader for 1 s and returns without calling `stderr.close()`, so that assertion fails and the reported leak remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:484 (`run_piped`)

chunk_findings.detail: The fake pipe assumes that `close()` from the caller thread unblocks another thread blocked in `read1`. A real `Popen.stderr` is a buffered file object/PIPE; on Linux, closing an fd in one thread does not reliably interrupt another thread blocked in `read(2)`. A patch that merely calls `p.stderr.close()` after the 1 s join would set `proc.stderr.closed` and pass this test, while the real stderr reader could remain blocked until a descendant closes the write end, so the regression test can certify a non-fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:18-38 (`_Pipe.read1`/`_Pipe.close`)

chunk_findings.detail: Closing `p.stderr` from the caller after `reader.join(1)` does not stop a reader already blocked in `read1`. On POSIX that call is inside the kernel `read` on the same fd; another thread's `close` does not abort it (and can race with fd reuse). `drain` only catches `ValueError`/`OSError` once `read1` returns, and `run_piped` never joins again before `return PipedEnd(...)`. Given a child that has exited while a descendant outside the process group still holds the stderr write end, `reader.is_alive()` stays true, the daemon thread keeps the `Popen` and both pipe ends referenced, and the leak this change claims to fix remains one object per call until that descendant exits. If `close` does make a later `read1` raise, `bytes(head)` still races with `drain`'s `head.extend` with no lock.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:94

chunk_findings.detail: The test’s contract is that an EOF reader “ends without a close,” but it never asserts `proc.stderr.closed is False` (or that the read fd was released). On the unfixed `run_piped` — join 1s, return, leave the pipe open — `EofPipe.read1` already returns `b""`, so this test passes both before and after the fix. It cannot fail the bug, and it blesses leaving the stderr fd open after a normal child exit, which is the same long-running leak the close-after-join fix is supposed to stop on the common path.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_reader_that_reaches_eof_ends_without_a_close
